** Which are the categories &c!'—i. e. which are the substances, which the properties, which the actions, and so forth.
And in as much as the cognitiou of the object does not necessarily
include the cognition of its qualifications, the further question
is added—" What are their similarities <&c" Herein also the
particle ' ca' has the collective force.
The Text supplies the answer to these questions : Among
these—i. e. among substance and the rest—the substances,
Earth and the rest, have beeu mentioned by the sätra, by their
general name of ' Substance,' as well as by their specific names,
'Earth,' 'Water/ &c.
Then there aiises the question as to whether these are the
only substances, or there are others also; and the Text
declares that they are nine only.}
Objection:—" The very fact of only nine substances being
defined would have shown clearly that there are only nine
substances ; and hence the addition of'nine only/ appears quite
superfluous."
Reply:—It is not so; as even though only nine would be
defined, yet «there would remain the doubt as to whether the
omission of others was due to the fact of there being uo others,
of to that of their being of no use (though existing). Specially
as all that the definition does is to aid ordinary usage by the
differentiation of the like from the unlike, and as such it could
not establish the non-existence of anything (besides the nine
substances): it is for this reason that we have the text
restricting the number of substances to ' nine only/
This specific mention of things that have been once mentioned by means of a generic term is what in ather systems is
called * Vibhäga' (Division), or lNirdeca' (Indication).
Question.—" How is it known that there are only nine
Substances ?".

19

Answer.—As besides tlieae none other is mentioned by
name.—That is to say, besides these nine, the great Rishij
Kanada, who was giving out his teaching with regard to all
things, his not mentioned (in his sutra) the name of any other.
P&ge $-1 Objection:—" There is a distinct substance in the
shape of Darkness {Tamas), which is endowed with the qualities
of colour, number, dimension, isolation, distance, proximity,
conjunction and disjunction."
To this some people make the following reply :—'If Darkness were a substance, then a person walking in the dark would
be obstructed by it; as a substance that has colour and form
can never be devoid of touch; aud a substance* that is large and
is endowed with touch is sure of offering an obstruction. Then
again, just as in the case of the Earth-globe, people are cognisant of its constituent parts, so should they also be of those of
Darkness.'
This answer is not quite satisfactory ; because in the case of
the light emitted by a lamp, we find that when certain rays of light
are thrown out from it, they give rise, through the force of a
certain unseen force, to an unimpeded circle of diffused light,
whose constituent parts are not perceived, and which is not
perceptible to the touch ; and in the same manner would the
substance of Darkness be constituted by the atoms of
Darkness (and would not be tangible).
For this reason, we offer another reply to the above argument (in favour of Darkness as a distinct substance) : Are the
atoms of Darkness endowed with touch, or devoid of it ? They
cannot be regarded as eadowed with it, as we never come across
any such products of it as wouM be perceptible by touch. It
nvght be argued that the said atom? do not produce any such
substances, because of the absence of an unseen force tending
towards such production. But., in that case, it would be equally
reasonable to accept Air to have colour; the absence of
coloured products of it being explained as being due to the

absence of the action of an unseen force favouring such production. Or, we might even assume all the four effect» ( Earth,
Water, Air and Light) to i»e produced from a single ato», through
the peculiar actioos of the unseen force.
It might be argued that, u the existence of atoms is
inferable only form their products ; and as such being inferred
from them, they cannot differ from these products; specially as
there would be no reasonable ground for admitting of such
difference."
But in that case, the atoms of Darkness also being devoid
of touch, how could they produce any such auhstauce as Dark*
ness ? as it is a fact of common experience th;»t that which is
without touch never producei any substances.
Objection :—'When we come across an effect, we naturally
assume the existence of a homogenous cause ; and it is not
right to upset or deny the character of the product to that which
is actually seen, simply because of some discrepancy in the
nature of its cause."
Reply :—We do not deny the existence of Darkness ; ail
that we assert is that, in as much as we do not find any productive cause for Darkness as a substance, and as all that we
actually see in Darkness is mere blacknessy it cannot be
regarded as a substance.
Obj: " In that case, Darkness would be cognised as mere
absence 0/light."
Reply: Not so; because any such mere absence of light
could never appear as black, endowed with the positive quality
of black colour ; while as a matter of fact, even at mid-day
we see darkness as black and moving and pervading over
things. Then again, in the case of all perception of negation
(or absence), we find that it is perceived only when its counterentity is perceived, and then too, through the negation of its
contrary, and as qualifiing something connected with that counter-entity ; and no absence is ever cognised independently by

itself. In the case of Darkness on the other hand, we find that
at the time that it is cognised, there.is no cognition of anything
eUe AS its counter-entity ; nor is its cognition in the form of a
negation. Consequently it canuot be regarded as the mere
absence of light.
Nor can its perception be regarded as one of light only; as
it is always outwardly cognised as 'darkness' and 'shadow',
and black in colour ( which can never apply to light which is by
its very nature ivhite). For these reasons, we must regard
darkness as a. particular colour (or form) which pervades on all
sides, when there is no light. And during the day too, the
blackness that is perceived is that enclosed above the eye-ball—
as we shall explain later on.
In a case where the ahsence of light occupies a fixed position, the blackness attaching to that place is cognised as 'shadow.'
It is for this reason that we have ideas of long, short, large and
small with reference to shadows; as that which is cognised is
the blackness extending over the place ( and as such capable of
being spoken of as ' longf &c.)
In case darkness be regarded as mere absence (of light), it
would be impossible to explain the application of such positive
epithets with regard f.o it. It is with a view to this that we
Lave the declaration—'Experienced people do not regard darkness
as mere absence of light; specially as the Puränas have spoken
of the bladcness of shadow, as a qualification of the earth. Then
again, in regard to shadows, we find that it follows in the wake
of the body (casting the shadow), and appears as distant and near
large and small, moving and standing,—all which would not be
possible unless it were a positive eutity.' It would also be difficult to explain the fact of the shadow being mistaken as a black
snake; and so also would be the notion of * moving', which is
caused by the cognition of colour; in places where there happens
to be an absence of light, the idea of motion is due to the
moving of the substance that shuts off the light (and casts the
shadow).

Similarly the ideas of Distance, Proximity, &c. in connection
with Darkness may he explained away (without necessitating the
assumption of an independent substance).
ID this perception of Darkness, which is a particular form
manifested by the absence of light, the perceptive potency
must be regarded as resting in the eye independent of the action
of any external light; as such perception is* always found tobe
concomitant with such an organ; just in the. same way as you
regard the. absence of light as the cause (<frf the perception
of Darkness).
Objection: "Such a theory would be contrary to the
Sütra which declares that darkness must be regarded as the
absence of light, because of the difference in the manifestation
of its substance, quality and action."
Reply: There is no contradiction; as Darkness has been
spoken of (in the Sütra) as the 'absence of light" simply because
it. is ouly in the absence of light that it is perceived.
( Mere difference in the number of qualities cannot justify
the admission of darkness as a distinct substance by itself; as)
God also being endowed with budhhit is accepted as ' self; and
the self wth six qualities (i.e the supreme Self)is not regarded as
wholly distinct from the self with fourteen qualities (i. e. the
human self); as any such distinction would be unreasonable in
view of the released human self (which having become merged
in the supreme Sell has only six. qualities).
KOTES.—Kuniärila and his followers maintain Darkness ( Tatnas } to be a
distinct substance. They argue that the moat general and accurate differentia
of Substances is that they are endowed with some pro per tie» and have some
sort of action ; and thta definition applies to Darkuess, which being black haa
the distinct quality of colour, and moves, thus having a definite action. It cannot
be included in any of the nine substances accepted by the Vaiqeshika. VaicesJiika
writers in general regard Darkness as mere absence of liyhtt and base their
rejection of the Mim >naaka theory on the ground that if Darkness had any
real colour it would require Light for its manifestation. This objection though
very plausible (n the surface loses its force when we come to look into the
matter a little deeper, and find that no Darkness can be perceived un'eas there
is light somewhere to see it off. But it is true that the Eye does not need the
aid of light in the perception of darkness. That is the reason why our Commentator has declared it to be a positive quality, perceptible by the eye in
dependency of the aid of light. The Prabhdkaras hold that Darkness is the absence
of the knowledge.^f light. Some extremists have gone to the length of denying
Light as a substance and holding it to be an absence of Darkness, which fatter
they accept as a substance. Some people have put forwaid cakti 'Force'as
a diatiuct substance ( Vide Nyäyamuktävali).

സൂത്രത്തിന്റെ ഉത്തരത്തിലെ 'ഏതാണ് ദ്രവ്യാദിപദാർത്ഥങ്ങൾ' എന്ന ചോദ്യത്തിന്റെ വിശദീകരണത്തിൽ ശ്രീധരൻ — ഏതാണു ദ്രവ്യങ്ങൾ, ഏതാണു ഗുണങ്ങൾ, ഏതാണു കർമ്മങ്ങൾ എന്നു വിശേഷിച്ചു — അവയുടെ സാധർമ്മ്യവൈധർമ്മ്യങ്ങളെ കൂടി പറയണം എന്നു ദ്യോതിപ്പിക്കുന്നു. ദ്രവ്യങ്ങൾ പൃഥിവി, ആപസ്സ്, തേജസ്സ്, വായു, ആകാശം, കാലം, ദിക്, ആത്മാ, മനസ്സ് — സാമാന്യസംജ്ഞയും വിശേഷസംജ്ഞയും കൊണ്ടു സൂത്രത്തിൽ ഉക്തങ്ങളായ — ഒൻപതെണ്ണം മാത്രം. പേർചൊല്ലി മറ്റൊന്നു ഇല്ലാത്തതുകൊണ്ടു ഒൻപതുമാത്രമെന്നു നിശ്ചയം.

പൂർവ്വപക്ഷം (മീമാംസകർ, പ്രത്യേകം കുമാരിലഭട്ടാദികൾ): തമസ്സ് — അന്ധകാരം — ഒരു സ്വതന്ത്രദ്രവ്യമത്രേ; അതിനു രൂപം, സംഖ്യ, പരിമാണം, പൃഥക്ത്വം, പരത്വം, അപരത്വം, സംയോഗം, വിഭാഗം എന്നീ ഗുണങ്ങൾ ഉണ്ടല്ലോ.

ചിലരുടെ ഉത്തരം: തമസ്സ് ദ്രവ്യമെങ്കിൽ, അന്ധകാരത്തിൽ നടക്കുന്നയാൾക്കു അതു പ്രതിബന്ധമാകേണ്ടതാണ് — രൂപമുള്ളതും വലിയ പരിമാണമുള്ളതുമായ ദ്രവ്യം സ്പർശമില്ലാത്തതാകില്ലല്ലോ. ഇതു അസമ്പൂർണ്ണപ്രതിവാദം.

ശരിയായ ഉത്തരം: അന്ധകാരത്തിന്റെ പരമാണുക്കൾക്കു സ്പർശം ഉണ്ടോ ഇല്ലയോ? ഉണ്ടെങ്കിൽ സ്പർശയോഗ്യമായ ഉത്പന്നം കാണാത്തതെന്ത്? ഇല്ലെങ്കിൽ — സ്പർശരഹിതദ്രവ്യം ദ്രവ്യാന്തരം ഉത്പാദിക്കില്ലല്ലോ. അതുകൊണ്ടു തമസ്സ് ദ്രവ്യമല്ല.

എങ്കിലും തമസ്സിന്റെ അസ്തിത്വം നിഷേധിക്കുന്നില്ല — ദ്രവ്യാന്തരത്തിന്റെ ഉത്പാദകത ഇല്ലാത്തതുകൊണ്ടും, തമസ്സിൽ കാണുന്നതു കേവലം 'കാളിമ'യാകയാലും — അതു ദ്രവ്യമല്ലെന്നു മാത്രം.

പ്രതിവാദം: 'എങ്കിൽ തമസ്സ് കേവലം ആലോകാഭാവമത്രേ.' ഉത്തരം: ആലോകാഭാവം കാളിമയോടെ പ്രകടമാകില്ലല്ലോ; മധ്യാഹ്നത്തിലും കാളിമ കണ്ടറിയാം. അഭാവത്തിന്റെ ജ്ഞാനം പ്രതിയോഗിജ്ഞാനത്തെ അനുവർത്തിച്ചു — നിഷേധരൂപമത്രേ; തമസ്സിൽ പ്രതിയോഗിജ്ഞാനവുമില്ല, നിഷേധരൂപവുമില്ല. അതുകൊണ്ടു തമസ്സ് ആലോകാഭാവമല്ല — ആലോകം ഇല്ലാത്തിടത്തു സർവ്വത്ര വ്യാപിക്കുന്ന ഒരുതരം 'വർണ്ണവിശേഷം' (കാളിമ) മാത്രമത്രേ.

ഛായാപ്രകരണത്തിലെ വ്യാഖ്യാനം: ആലോകാഭാവം നിശ്ചിതസ്ഥാനത്തു ഉണ്ടാകുമ്പോൾ ആ സ്ഥാനത്തുള്ള കാളിമ 'ഛായ' എന്നു വ്യപദേശിക്കപ്പെടുന്നു. 'ദീർഘച്ഛായ', 'ലഘുച്ഛായ' എന്നീ വിശേഷണങ്ങൾ ഇതുകൊണ്ടത്രേ.

നേത്രേന്ദ്രിയം ബാഹ്യാലോകത്തിന്റെ സഹായം ഇല്ലാതെ തന്നെ കാളിമയെ ഗ്രഹിക്കാൻ ശക്തമത്രേ — സ്വാഭാവികമായ പ്രത്യക്ഷശക്തി. സൂത്രവിരോധമെന്നു തോന്നുമെങ്കിലും — സൂത്രത്തിൽ 'ആലോകാഭാവ'മെന്നു പറഞ്ഞതു തമസ്സ് ആലോകം ഇല്ലാത്തിടത്തു മാത്രമേ ഗ്രഹിക്കപ്പെടുന്നുള്ളൂ എന്നതുകൊണ്ടു മാത്രമത്രേ.

Śrīdhara opens the chapter on enumeration with a careful parsing of the *mūla*'s question: "Which are the *padārtha*s — *dravya* and the rest?" means: which are the *dravya*s, which the *guṇa*s, which the *karma*s, and so on. The *sūtra* lists the *dravya*s by both *sāmānya-saṃjñā* ("substance") and *viśeṣa-saṃjñā* ("earth", "water" etc.), and limits them to nine because no other has been named.

The bulk of the commentary is given to refuting the Mīmāṃsaka claim (notably Kumārila and his school) that *tamas* (darkness) is a tenth *dravya*, possessing colour, number, dimension, separateness, distance, proximity, conjunction, and disjunction.

*Pūrvapakṣa*: Darkness, having a black colour and acting as a substrate of various qualities, must itself be a *dravya*.

*Siddhānta*: First a weaker rebuttal — if darkness were a *dravya* it would obstruct one who walks through it, since coloured large *dravya*s always have *sparśa*. Śrīdhara himself rejects this argument because the Mīmāṃsaka can reply that light rays form a visible but intangible diffused circle, so atoms of darkness could likewise be intangible. The real reply runs through the atoms: are *tamas* *paramāṇu*s touch-bearing or not? If yes, why no touch-bearing products? If no, an untouched substance cannot generate any substantial product. Either way *tamas* is not a *dravya*.

But Śrīdhara grants the phenomenon. What we call *tamas* is not a *dravya* but a particular kind of black colour (*kāla-rūpa-viśeṣa*) that pervades wherever there is *āloka-abhāva* (absence of light). Nor is it merely the absence of light: an *abhāva* is grasped only alongside its *pratiyogin* (counter-correlate) and in negative form, while darkness is grasped positively, with its own blackness, even at noon. Shadow is just blackness occupying a fixed region — hence we speak of "long shadow", "short shadow".

The *cakṣur-indriya* (eye-organ) is granted a natural capacity to perceive this *kāla-rūpa* without the aid of external light, which answers the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra*'s description of *tamas* as *āloka-abhāva*: the *sūtra* is saying only that *tamas* is grasped where light is absent, not that *tamas* is mere absence.

The seventeen qualities, Colour and the rest, have been,
distinctly named in the Sütra, and the word ' ca' indicates the
others, Gravity &c, which are ordinarily recognised as * qualities.' Thus the number of Qualities is twenty-four only. As
for the qualities of Bravery, Magnanimity, Compassion, Cleverness, Vanity and the like, all these are included in the aforesaid
twentyf»iur. For instance, Bravery is nothing more than an
inclination towards the subjugation of an enemy, even if he be
stronger than oneself; Magnanimity consists of the Intellect
as always tending towards the right path; Compassion is the
desire to alleviate th.3 sufferings of others ; Cleverness lies in
the Intellect directed towards the real state of things; Vanity
consists in an exaggerated idea of one's own greatness; and so
forth. The word ' adiyhta' (Invisible Force) includes virtue
and vice (dharma and adhamvt). The word (Sahslcdra*
(Faculty) includes speed, memory and elasticity.
Ohj: " If these words were to iüclude all these qualities,
then the number of Qualities would exeeod twenty-four."
Reyly: Not so; because all these three—viz. speed
meir.ory and elasticity—belong to the same class of( Faculty/ and
are regarded as oue only.
Objection: " In that case, the number of qualities would
not be twenty-four; as both Virtue and Vice belonging to the
same class of ' Adrshta' would also be regarded as one only."

 21

PRAQASTAPADA BHASHYA—CHAP. II. SECTlOSf(I).

Reply: Not so; as there is no such class as ' adrshta*
Though the Qualities themselves are devoid of qualities (and
as such they could not be qualified by the number 'twenty-four'-,
yet they are spoken of as ' twenty-four,'—the number being applied to them indirectly, by reason of their being capable of
having distinctive features of their own (the number rea'ly
belonging to these features, and through them transferred to the
Qualities themselves).
NOTES. —(1) Quality ig defined as that which, being neither substance vor
action, is capable of generalities ; or, thac which, while inhering in substances,
is devoid of quality and action. Kanada ( Vaiqeskikasutra, I-i-l6) has defined
it as that which inhering in substances. 13 devoid of qualities, and ia an independent cause of conjunctions and disjunctions. It differs from Substance in
that, while the latter is capable of existing independently by itself, Quality can
never exist apart from Substance. And though Quality aud Action both inhe.e
i« Substance, the furtner is a per.i anent factor tu substances while the latter ia
evanescent. "We understand by Quality thac which truly constitutes the nature
of a thing—what it is,—what belongs to it permanently as a» individual or in
common with others like it,—not that which passes, which vanishes and answers
o no lasting judgment. A body falls: it i« a fact, an accident ; it ia heavy,,
that is quality "
(2) We meet with extensive discussions in various works as to the propriety
of the twenty-four—fold classification of qualities. But there is a general
agreement on the point that all qualities are included, in one way or the other,
in those enumerated among the twenty-four.
(3) Qualities are divided—(a) into Eternal and Evanescent, (b) into General
and Specific, and (c) coguisable by one aen»e, by two senses, or not cognisable by »
seuse organs.
(a) Those belonging
to eternal substances are eternal, and those in transient
substance3, evanescent.
(b) The General qualities are those that subsist conjointly in two or more
substances while the speci;c quality is that residing in only one
substance.
(c) The qualities apprehended by single sense-organs are colour, taste,
odjur and touch; those cognisable by two sense organs are dimension,
separateness, conjunction, disjunction, distance, proximity, lluidity
*nd viscidity; the super-sensuous are gravity, ad harm a, dharuaa and

ശൗര്യം — ശ്രേഷ്ഠശത്രുവിനെ പരാജയിപ്പിക്കാനുള്ള പ്രവൃത്തിസ്വഭാവം. ഔദാര്യം — ന്യായമാർഗ്ഗത്തിലെ ബുദ്ധി. ദയ — അന്യദുഃഖനിവൃത്തിയിലെ ഇച്ഛ. ചാതുര്യം — യഥാർത്ഥവസ്തുബുദ്ധി. ദർപ്പം — ആത്മാധിക്യബുദ്ധി. 'അദൃഷ്ടം' ധർമ്മാധർമ്മങ്ങളെ ഉൾക്കൊള്ളുന്നു. 'സംസ്കാരം' വേഗം, സ്മൃതി, സ്ഥിതിസ്ഥാപകത എന്നിവയെ.

പൂർവ്വപക്ഷം: 'വേഗം, സ്മൃതി, സ്ഥിതിസ്ഥാപകത മൂന്നു വേറെ വേറെ ഗുണങ്ങളെങ്കിൽ, ഇരുപത്തിനാല് എണ്ണത്തിൽ കവിയില്ലേ?' ഉത്തരം: മൂന്നും ഒരേ 'സംസ്കാര'ജാതിയിലെ വിശേഷങ്ങളാകയാൽ, ഏകം മാത്രം.

പ്രതിപൂർവ്വപക്ഷം: 'അദൃഷ്ടം ധർമ്മാധർമ്മാദിയിലെ ഉത്കൃഷ്ടവിശേഷങ്ങളെങ്കിൽ — ഏകജാത്യാത്മകത്വം സ്ഥിരമല്ലല്ലോ.' ഉത്തരം: 'അദൃഷ്ടം' എന്ന ഒരു ജാതി ഇല്ല; ധർമ്മാധർമ്മങ്ങൾ വേറെ വേറെ ഗുണവിശേഷങ്ങൾ തന്നെ.

ഗുണങ്ങൾ സ്വയം ഗുണരഹിതങ്ങളെങ്കിലും, വൈശേഷ്യം നിമിത്തം 'ഇരുപത്തിനാല്' എന്ന സംഖ്യ ഉപചാരേണ ആരോപിക്കപ്പെടുന്നു — സംഖ്യ വാസ്തവത്തിൽ വൈശേഷ്യങ്ങളിലത്രേ, ഗുണങ്ങളിലല്ല.

Praśastapāda has enumerated seventeen *guṇa*s explicitly in the *sūtra* and seven more (gravity, fluidity, viscidity, *saṃskāra*, the twofold *adṛṣṭa*, and *śabda*) implied by the particle *ca*. Śrīdhara's task is to defend the twenty-four count.

He absorbs popular *guṇa*-words into the canonical list: bravery is a *pravṛtti* aimed at defeating a stronger enemy; magnanimity is *buddhi* tending toward the right path; compassion is *icchā* directed at the relief of others' suffering; cleverness is *buddhi* fixed on what is really the case; vanity is an inflated *buddhi* about oneself. *adṛṣṭa* covers *dharma* and *adharma*; *saṃskāra* covers speed (*vega*), memory (*smṛti*) and elasticity (*sthiti-sthāpaka*).

*Pūrvapakṣa*: If *saṃskāra* contains three sub-qualities, the total exceeds twenty-four. *Siddhānta*: All three belong to one class, *saṃskāra*, so they count as one. *Pūrvapakṣin* again: Then by parity *dharma* and *adharma* should also count as one under *adṛṣṭa*. Reply: there is no *jāti* called *adṛṣṭa*; *dharma* and *adharma* are two distinct *guṇa-viśeṣa*s. 

Finally, *guṇa*s themselves are *nirguṇa*, so strictly they cannot bear the number twenty-four; the number is applied secondarily, *upacāra*-style, because each *guṇa* admits of distinguishing features.

*Antya-viśeṣa*s — the ultimate individuators — inhere in *nitya-dravya*s alone. The qualification "inhering in *nitya-dravya*s alone" excludes *dravya*, *guṇa*, *karma* and *sāmānya*: the first three inhere in *dravya* generally but not exclusively in *nitya-dravya*, and *sāmānya* is not restricted to *dravya* at all. The qualification "sure to inhere" excludes *buddhi*, *śabda* and the like, which do not pervade all *nitya-dravya*s.

*Pūrvapakṣa*: Are *viśeṣa*s also *sāmānya* (like *dravya*-ness, which is both *sāmānya* and *viśeṣa*) or pure *viśeṣa*? *Siddhānta*: The particle *khalu* ("certainly") settles it: they are *viśeṣa* purely and never relapse into *sāmānya*, for their only function is the absolute exclusion (*atyanta-vyāvṛtti*) of their substrate from every other.

The author proceeds to explain the nature of Inherence.
'Yutasiddi* is separate existence, the existence of two relative
things apart from each other ; those that have no such separate existence are ' ayutasiddhas'; and it is the relationship
of these that is known as 'Inherence \ e.g. the relationship
betweeu the Cloth and the Yarns composing it; though the
Yarns have an independent existence of their own, apart from
the Cloth (Jit. inhere in substrates other than the Cloth), yet the
mutual relationship between the Yarn and the Cloth is such
that they do not bear the relationship of the container and the
contained to anything else (i. e. have no existence apart from
each other). It is only when the two factors are so related that
each bears to the other the relationship of the container and the

Touch. Consequently the relationship in this latter case, would

In the case of two eternal substances, * yutasiddhi' would

which is one of- cause and effect,—would also become 'Inherence';

സമവായം എന്നുള്ളതു അയുതസിദ്ധങ്ങളായ (പരസ്പരം വേർപെടാത്ത) ആധാര്യാധാരസ്ഥിതങ്ങളായ വസ്തുക്കളുടെ സംബന്ധമത്രേ — 'ഇതിൽ ഇതുണ്ടു' എന്ന ഇഹപ്രത്യയത്തിന്റെ ഹേതുവായതു. 'യുതസിദ്ധി' വേർപെട്ടു സ്ഥിതിയോഗ്യത്വം — ദണ്ഡിയും ദണ്ഡവുമെന്നു പറയും പോലെ. അയുതസിദ്ധി — സ്വരൂപവൈകല്യം ഇല്ലാതെ പരസ്പരവേർപാടു അസാദ്ധ്യമായതു: അവയവിയും അവയവവും, ഗുണവും ഗുണിയും, ക്രിയയും ക്രിയാവാനും, ജാതിയും വ്യക്തിയും, വിശേഷങ്ങളും നിത്യദ്രവ്യങ്ങളും.

സംയോഗത്തിൽ — യുതസിദ്ധങ്ങളിലെ താൽക്കാലികസംബന്ധം — സമവായം പ്രസക്തമല്ല. സമവായം ഏകം — ഒരേ സ്വരൂപമത്രേ സർവ്വസമവായികളിലും. പൂർവ്വപക്ഷം: 'ഭിന്നഭിന്നസമവായം — നൂറുകണക്കിന് സമവായം — ഉണ്ടാകണം.' ഉത്തരം: അനന്തബാധകം; ഏകസമവായവിശ്വാസത്തിൽ ദോഷം ഇല്ല.

സമവായം 'ഭാവം' തന്നെ — ഭിന്നപദാർത്ഥമത്രേ; ഗുണാദിയിൽ അന്തർഭവിക്കില്ല. ഗുണത്തിന്റെ ലക്ഷണം ദ്രവ്യാശ്രയത്വം — സമവായം ദ്രവ്യാശ്രയം മാത്രമല്ലല്ലോ. കർമ്മത്തിന്റെ ലക്ഷണവും സമവായത്തിൽ ബാധിതം. അതുകൊണ്ടു സമവായം ഷഷ്ഠപദാർത്ഥം തന്നെ.

സമവായം പ്രത്യക്ഷഗ്രാഹ്യമല്ല — അനുമേയം. 'ഇഹ കുണ്ഡേ ദധി' എന്നുപോലെ 'ഇഹ തന്തുഷു പട'ഃ എന്ന ഇഹപ്രത്യയത്തിന്റെ വിശേഷണത്വം നിമിത്തം. അനുമാനം: ഈ ഇഹപ്രത്യയത്തിനു സംയോഗവ്യതിരിക്തമായ നിയാമകസംബന്ധം ഉണ്ടു — സംയോഗം പിന്നെ യുതസിദ്ധങ്ങളിലത്രേ — അതുകൊണ്ടു ഈ സംബന്ധം സമവായമത്രേ.

സമവായം നിത്യം — കാരണാന്തരം ഇല്ലാത്തതുകൊണ്ടു. അനന്തസമവായാപത്തി ('സമവായത്തിന്റെ സമവായം' ഇത്യാദി) വരാതെ — സമവായം സ്വസ്വരൂപേണ തന്നെ പട-തന്തുവിൽ വർത്തിക്കുന്നതാകയാൽ — സ്വാത്മനി തന്നെ വർത്തനം. ഏതെങ്കിലും വസ്തു സ്വാത്മനി വർത്തിക്കാമെങ്കിലേ ഇതരത്തിൽ സമവായരൂപേണ വർത്തിക്കാൻ ശക്യം എന്നു ന്യായം.

en_simple_draft.text:
*Samavāya* — inseparable inherence — is the relation between two *ayuta-siddha* terms standing as *ādhāra* (locus) and *ādheya* (located), and it grounds the *iha-pratyaya* ("this is in that"). *Yuta-siddhi* is the capacity to stand apart while retaining one's form (the man and his staff). *Ayuta-siddhi* is the opposite: the parts and whole, *guṇa* and its substrate, *kriyā* and the agent, *jāti* and the individual, *antya-viśeṣa* and *nitya-dravya* — none of these can subsist without the other.

Therefore *saṃyoga* — the temporary contact of *yuta-siddha* things — is excluded from *samavāya*. *Samavāya* is **one**, having a single form everywhere; the alternative — many separate *samavāya*s, one per instance — would entail an *anavasthā* (endless multiplicity).

*Samavāya* is a *bhāva* — a positive entity, distinct from *guṇa*, *karma* and the rest. *Guṇa* always rests in *dravya* only; *samavāya* does not. *Karma* shares the same defect. Hence *samavāya* is a *padārtha* in its own right.

*Samavāya* is not *pratyakṣa* (directly perceived) but *anumeya* (inferred). From the cognition "the cloth (rests) in these threads" ("*iha tantuṣu paṭaḥ*"), which is the pattern of *iha-pratyaya*, we infer a relation distinct from *saṃyoga* (since *saṃyoga* belongs only to *yuta-siddha* relata). That relation is *samavāya*.

*Samavāya* is *nitya* (eternal), as it has no productive cause. The regress threatened by "*samavāya* of *samavāya*" is blocked because *samavāya* itself stands in its substrate by its own form (*sva-svarūpa-vṛtti*), not by a further *samavāya*. To resist the regress, one item must be self-residing; that item is *samavāya* itself.

പദാർത്ഥങ്ങളെ പേർ ചൊല്ലി ഉദ്ദേശിച്ചതുകൊണ്ടു ധർമ്മങ്ങളെ പ്രതിപാദിക്കാൻ പര്യാപ്തമായില്ലല്ലോ. അതുകൊണ്ടു — കാര്യാന്തരത്തെ പ്രസ്താവിക്കാൻ — കർത്താവ് മുൻഭാഗവുമായുള്ള സംബന്ധം സൂചിപ്പിക്കുന്നു: മുൻഭാഗത്തു പേർ പറഞ്ഞു മാത്രമേ ഇരുന്നുള്ളൂ — ഇനി ധർമ്മങ്ങളെ പറയും.

ദ്രവ്യാദികളുടെ ഉപവിഭാഗങ്ങൾ പറഞ്ഞെങ്കിലും അവയും കേവലനാമോദ്ദേശമത്രേ; 'കേവലോദ്ദേശ'ത്തിൽ അന്തർഭവിക്കുന്നു.

കിരണാവലിയിലെ വ്യാഖ്യാനം: 'പിന്നെ ശക്തി, സാദൃശ്യാദികളെ എന്തുകൊണ്ടു പറഞ്ഞില്ല?' എന്ന ആക്ഷേപത്തിന്റെ ഉത്തരം ഈ പാഠം — ഇതുവരെ ഉദ്ദേശിച്ചതു പദാർത്ഥങ്ങൾ മാത്രമത്രേ; ശക്തിയും സാദൃശ്യവും ധർമ്മങ്ങളിൽ പെടും.

en_simple_draft.text:
Since the categories have so far been mentioned only by name, a discussion of their *dharma*s could not yet begin. The author therefore now signals the transition: "In what has come before we have stated the *padārtha*s by name only; we now turn to their properties." Even the sub-divisions of *dravya* and the rest have been only *nāma-uddeśa* and so fall under the same heading of "mere mention".

The *Kiraṇāvalī* takes this *mūla* as Praśastapāda's answer to the objection "why have only these six been enumerated, and not *śakti*, *sādṛśya*, and the like?" — namely that only the categories have been named; *śakti* and *sādṛśya* fall under the *dharma*s yet to be discussed.
